Do not specify Class 3 for cost reasons or perceived quality improvement; the cost and lead time increase is significant and the additional reliability is only needed in specific applications.

Document the IPC class on the fabrication and assembly drawings. Include specific callouts for any criteria where you need to deviate from the class default (e.g., Class 2 board with Class 3 annular ring on specific nets, or specific solder joint criteria for safety-critical connections).

description: Layout a mixed-signal PCB: resolve the ground partitioning question, design guard rings, optimize ADC/DAC placement for SNR, and mitigate substrate coupling.

steps.description: Resolve the analog/digital ground split vs single ground plane debate using the actual physics of return current flow and current density.

inputs.name: circuit-topology
inputs.desc: Schematic showing analog and digital sections, their interconnections, and the ADC/DAC bridge points

inputs.name: signal-frequencies
inputs.desc: Analog signal bandwidth and digital clock frequencies

inputs.name: noise-budget
inputs.desc: Allowable noise on the analog signals in LSBs or microvolts

outputs.name: ground-strategy
outputs.desc: Single ground plane with controlled current flow, or split ground with defined bridge point, with the engineering rationale

outputs.name: current-flow-map
outputs.desc: Map showing where digital return currents flow and where analog signals are sensitive, identifying any overlap

outputs.name: partition-implementation
outputs.desc: Physical implementation: moat location (if split), bridge point location, stitching via placement

process: Start with the principle: a solid, unbroken ground plane has the lowest impedance and is the default correct answer. A split ground plane is only correct when digital return currents would flow through the analog measurement area AND you can guarantee that no signal trace crosses the split.

Map the digital return current paths: for each digital signal, the return current flows on the nearest ground plane directly under the trace (at high frequency, return current follows the signal trace path, not the shortest DC path). Identify where these return current paths overlap with the analog signal area.

If digital return currents do not flow through the analog area (the digital section is physically separated), a single ground plane is correct. Connect analog and digital ground at a single point (the ADC/DAC ground pin). This is not a split; it is a star connection on a single plane.

If digital return currents must flow through the analog area (compact layout, cannot separate sections), consider a moat: a slot in the ground plane that forces digital return currents to flow around the analog section. The moat must not be crossed by any trace (signal or power). Connect the two sides of the moat at one point, directly under the ADC/DAC. This is the classic split-ground approach and is only correct when the moat can be kept inviolate.

steps.description: Design guard rings and guard traces to protect sensitive analog nodes from leakage current, noise coupling, and field pickup.

inputs.name: ground-strategy
inputs.desc: Ground approach from partitioning step

inputs.name: sensitive-nodes
inputs.desc: Nodes requiring protection: high-impedance inputs, reference voltages, low-level analog signals

inputs.name: noise-budget
inputs.desc: Maximum tolerable noise per sensitive node

outputs.name: guard-ring-design
outputs.desc: Guard ring for each sensitive node: ring potential (driven or grounded), width, clearance to the sensitive trace, and connection to the circuit

outputs.name: layout-rules-for-analog
outputs.desc: Routing rules: minimum clearance from digital traces, maximum trace length for sensitive signals, via rules for analog connections

outputs.name: shielding-requirements
outputs.desc: Whether a ground pour, shield can, or Faraday cage is needed for specific sensitive areas

process: For high-impedance nodes (> 10 Mohm, such as photodiode amplifier inputs): surface leakage on the PCB can inject picoamps to nanoamps of current. A guard ring driven to the same potential as the sensitive node (by the op-amp output in a follower configuration) intercepts surface leakage current. The guard ring must completely surround the sensitive node on all PCB layers that the node touches.

For reference voltage nodes: surround with a ground guard ring (connected to the local analog ground) to prevent noise coupling from nearby digital or switching traces. The guard ring width should be at least 20 mils and connected to ground with vias every 100 mils to maintain low impedance at high frequency.

Set routing rules for analog signals: keep analog traces at least 3x the trace width away from digital traces (5x for sensitive signals). Keep analog traces short (minimize antenna pickup length). Route analog signals on internal layers between ground planes when possible (stripline provides natural shielding). Use vias sparingly for analog signals (each via adds parasitic inductance and can create a stub).

For the most sensitive circuits (microvolts, nanoamps): consider a metal shield can soldered over the sensitive area. The shield can connects to the ground plane through multiple vias and provides 30 to 60 dB of additional isolation from radiated interference. Alternatively, use a ground pour on the layer above and below the sensitive circuit (a PCB Faraday cage).

steps.description: Layout ADC and DAC circuits for maximum SNR and minimum distortion, applying the converter manufacturer's recommendations with the physics behind them.

inputs.name: partition-implementation
inputs.desc: Ground strategy implementation

inputs.name: guard-ring-design
inputs.desc: Protection for sensitive nodes

inputs.name: component-datasheets
inputs.desc: ADC/DAC datasheets with layout recommendations and evaluation board layout

outputs.name: adc-dac-placement
outputs.desc: Component placement for each converter: decoupling capacitor positions, reference circuit location, input network placement

outputs.name: critical-trace-routing
outputs.desc: Routing plan for clock, analog input, reference, and digital output traces with length and spacing constraints

outputs.name: performance-verification-plan
outputs.desc: How to verify the layout achieves the datasheet SNR: test points, measurement method, expected degradation from layout

process: Place the ADC/DAC decoupling capacitors first, before any other component in the area. Each AVDD pin gets a 100 nF capacitor within 2 mm, connected directly to the AGND pin (not to a distant ground via). Each DVDD pin gets a 100 nF capacitor connected to DGND. A 10 uF bulk capacitor serves each power domain. These capacitor positions are non-negotiable; other components route around them.

Place the voltage reference circuit adjacent to the ADC reference pins. The reference decoupling capacitor must be within 3 mm of the REF pin. Route the reference trace as a wide (20 mil minimum), short, direct connection. Any noise on the reference appears directly as gain error in every sample. Shield the reference trace between ground traces or on a shielded internal layer.

Route the ADC clock as a controlled-impedance trace, matched to the clock source impedance (usually 50 ohms). Keep the clock trace away from analog input traces (10 mm minimum separation or on different layers with a ground plane between them). Clock jitter degrades SNR: a 1 ps rms jitter on a 100 MHz input signal costs 1 dB of SNR. The clock trace is as critical as the analog input.

Route digital output traces away from analog inputs. The digital outputs switch during each conversion and create transient currents in the ground plane. Route digital outputs toward the digital section, away from the analog section. If the ADC has a serial output (SPI, LVDS), prefer it over parallel outputs because fewer traces switch simultaneously, creating less ground bounce.

steps.description: Layout a crystal oscillator circuit for reliable startup, frequency accuracy, and minimum EMI.

inputs.name: crystal-parameters
inputs.desc: Crystal frequency, load capacitance, ESR, and drive level

inputs.name: oscillator-ic
inputs.desc: IC with oscillator pins (XTAL_IN, XTAL_OUT) and its recommended circuit

inputs.name: emc-emi-requirements
inputs.desc: EMI constraints on the clock circuit

outputs.name: crystal-placement
outputs.desc: Crystal position relative to IC, load capacitor positions, and ground connection

outputs.name: routing-rules
outputs.desc: Trace length, width, and spacing rules for XTAL_IN and XTAL_OUT traces

outputs.name: emi-mitigation
outputs.desc: Guard ring or ground pour design around the crystal circuit for EMI containment

process: Place the crystal as close to the IC oscillator pins as physically possible (5 mm maximum for most crystals, 3 mm for high-frequency crystals above 25 MHz). The traces from IC to crystal must be short because they carry a high-impedance, low-amplitude signal that is susceptible to noise pickup and adds parasitic capacitance that detunes the oscillator.

Place the load capacitors (CL1, CL2) directly at the crystal pads, connected to ground through short, dedicated ground vias. These capacitors set the oscillator frequency: C_load = (CL1 * CL2) / (CL1 + CL2) must equal the crystal's specified load capacitance minus the parasitic capacitance of the traces and IC pins (typically 3 to 5 pF). Getting this wrong shifts the frequency and can prevent startup.

Route XTAL_IN and XTAL_OUT as short, direct traces. Do not route them as parallel traces (couple noise between them). Keep them away from all other signals, especially digital clocks and switching regulators. A 10 mil minimum clearance from other traces, 50 mil from noisy signals. Do not put vias in the crystal traces; route on a single layer.

Surround the crystal circuit with a ground guard pour on the same layer, connected to the ground plane with vias every 50 to 100 mils. This contains the crystal's EMI (the crystal is a narrow-band radiator at its fundamental frequency and harmonics) and shields the circuit from external noise. Do not route any other signal through this ground pour.

steps.description: Layout power supply circuits for correct sequencing, minimizing coupling between regulators, and ensuring each supply has a clean, isolated ground return.

inputs.name: power-tree
inputs.desc: Power supply tree showing all regulators, their inputs, outputs, and sequencing requirements

inputs.name: ground-strategy
inputs.desc: Ground partitioning approach

inputs.name: component-datasheets
inputs.desc: Regulator datasheets with layout recommendations

outputs.name: regulator-placement-plan
outputs.desc: Physical placement of each regulator optimized for thermal management and minimizing output-to-input coupling

outputs.name: sequencing-circuit-layout
outputs.desc: Layout of sequencing and enable circuits ensuring signal integrity on enable/power-good nets

outputs.name: supply-isolation-verification
outputs.desc: Verification that each supply's input and output decoupling are isolated from other supplies' noise

process: Place switching regulators away from sensitive analog circuits. The switching node (where the inductor connects to the FET) radiates at the switching frequency and harmonics. Maintain at least 10 mm between a switching regulator's inductor and any sensitive analog component. If closer placement is unavoidable, orient the inductor's magnetic axis perpendicular to the sensitive circuit.

For each switching regulator: place the input capacitor, boot capacitor, and output capacitor according to the datasheet's recommended layout. The input capacitor to high-side FET to low-side FET to ground loop must be minimized (this is the hot loop that radiates). The output capacitor placement is less critical for EMI but important for output ripple.

Route power-good and enable signals as controlled signals, not afterthoughts. These signals determine sequencing order and timing. A noisy enable signal can cause false startup or glitched sequencing. Route enable signals away from switching nodes and high-di/dt traces. Add a 100 nF bypass capacitor at the enable pin if the trace is longer than 25 mm.

Verify supply isolation: each regulator's input decoupling capacitor should sit between the input trace and the regulator, not shared with other regulators. If two regulators share an input rail, each must have its own local input capacitor. The return current from each regulator's output should flow back to its own output capacitor and then to its own input capacitor, not through another regulator's ground path.

description: Design flex and rigid-flex PCBs: bend radius calculation, material selection for static vs dynamic flex, controlled impedance in flex regions, and reliability at rigid-to-flex transitions.

steps.description: Classify the flex application as static (bend once during assembly), dynamic (repeated bending in use), or flex-to-install, and select the design rules accordingly.

inputs.name: application-description
inputs.desc: How the flex will be used: hinge, cable replacement, fold for packaging, connector elimination

inputs.name: bend-cycles
inputs.desc: Expected number of bend cycles over product lifetime

inputs.name: bend-angle
inputs.desc: Maximum bend angle required in degrees

outputs.name: flex-classification
outputs.desc: Static flex (< 25 bends), flex-to-install (25 to 1000 bends), or dynamic flex (> 1000 bends)

outputs.name: design-rule-set
outputs.desc: Which IPC-2223 design rules apply: copper type, layer count limits, bend radius multipliers

outputs.name: material-constraints
outputs.desc: Copper type (rolled annealed for dynamic, electrodeposited acceptable for static), adhesive requirements, coverlay vs solder mask

process: Count expected bend cycles over the product lifetime. Include assembly, service, and in-use bending. A laptop hinge that opens and closes 10 times per day for 5 years sees 18,000 cycles: that is dynamic flex and needs the most conservative design rules.

Classify: static flex allows more layers, tighter bend radius, and electrodeposited (ED) copper. Dynamic flex requires rolled annealed (RA) copper (ductile, survives repeated bending), fewer layers (ideally single-layer in the bend zone), and larger bend radius.

Select copper type: RA copper has an elongation of 20 to 30%, meaning it can stretch that much before cracking. ED copper has 5 to 10% elongation. In a dynamic flex application, the outer copper layer experiences tensile strain = t / (2 * R + t) where t is total stackup thickness and R is bend radius. This strain must stay below the copper's fatigue limit for the required cycle count.

Select coverlay vs solder mask: flexible coverlay (polyimide film adhesive-bonded over the traces) is required for all flex regions. Liquid photoimageable solder mask is too brittle for flex regions and will crack, exposing copper to corrosion and fatigue. Solder mask is used only in rigid sections and stiffened areas.

steps.description: Calculate the minimum bend radius from material properties, layer count, and copper thickness, and design the flex stackup to meet it.

inputs.name: flex-classification
inputs.desc: Static, flex-to-install, or dynamic

inputs.name: material-constraints
inputs.desc: Copper type and coverlay requirements

inputs.name: layer-count-in-flex
inputs.desc: Number of copper layers that pass through the bend zone

inputs.name: copper-weight
inputs.desc: Copper weight on each layer in the bend zone

outputs.name: minimum-bend-radius
outputs.desc: Calculated minimum bend radius in mm for the required cycle life

outputs.name: flex-stackup
outputs.desc: Layer stackup in the flex region: copper layers, adhesive layers, polyimide substrate layers, with total thickness

outputs.name: neutral-axis-location
outputs.desc: Position of the mechanical neutral axis and whether copper layers are balanced above and below it

process: Calculate total flex thickness: sum all layers in the bend zone (copper, adhesive, polyimide substrate, coverlay). For a single-layer flex: 12 um copper + 25 um polyimide + 25 um coverlay adhesive + 25 um coverlay polyimide = 87 um total.

Apply the IPC-2223 bend radius rule: minimum bend radius = thickness * multiplier. For single-layer dynamic flex, the multiplier is 10 (R_min = 10 * t). For dual-layer dynamic flex, the multiplier is 15 to 20. For static flex, the multiplier is 6 for single-layer. These are conservative minimums.

Verify copper strain at the minimum bend radius: strain = t_total / (2 * R_bend). For 87 um thickness at R = 0.87 mm (10x multiplier): strain = 0.087 / (2 * 0.87 + 0.087) = 4.8%. RA copper's fatigue limit for 100,000 cycles is approximately 0.3% strain. So 10x is not enough for true dynamic flex at high cycle count; increase to 25x or 50x for > 10,000 cycles.

Balance the stackup about the neutral axis: place copper layers symmetrically. In a 2-layer flex, put one copper layer above and one below the polyimide core so the neutral axis falls between them. An unbalanced stackup puts copper at the maximum strain position (outermost surface), doubling the strain compared to a balanced design.

steps.description: Design the transition zone where rigid and flex sections meet, preventing stress concentration and delamination.

inputs.name: flex-stackup
inputs.desc: Flex region layer stack

inputs.name: minimum-bend-radius
inputs.desc: Bend radius driving transition zone length

inputs.name: rigid-stackup
inputs.desc: Rigid section layer stack (more layers than flex)

outputs.name: transition-zone-design
outputs.desc: Geometry of the rigid-to-flex transition: taper angle, stiffener overlap, strain relief features

outputs.name: copper-routing-in-transition
outputs.desc: How traces are routed through the transition: staggered via placement, tear-stop features, keepout zones

outputs.name: stiffener-specification
outputs.desc: Stiffener material, thickness, and adhesive for areas requiring mechanical support in the flex region

process: The transition zone is the highest-stress area in a rigid-flex board. The abrupt change from rigid (thick, stiff) to flex (thin, flexible) creates a stress concentration at the boundary. All cracking failures in rigid-flex start here.

Design the transition with a gradual taper: the rigid section should taper toward the flex over a distance of at least 2.5 mm (IPC-2223 minimum). The taper can be achieved by stepping the rigid layers back from the flex boundary, so each layer ends at a different point.

Add tear-stop features: anchor the flex layers to the rigid section with tear-stop vias or slots at the transition boundary. These prevent the flex material from tearing or delaminating at the stress concentration. Place a row of vias 0.5 mm inside the rigid section, parallel to the flex boundary.

Route traces through the transition zone perpendicular to the flex boundary (not at an angle). Avoid vias within 1 mm of the transition boundary on the flex side. Stagger via locations (not in a straight line across the transition) to avoid creating a perforation line that could crack. In the flex region adjacent to the transition, do not place components for at least 2 mm to allow the flex to bend freely.

steps.description: Achieve controlled impedance in flex sections despite the different dielectric properties and thinner construction.

inputs.name: flex-stackup
inputs.desc: Flex region materials and thicknesses

inputs.name: signal-classes
inputs.desc: Signals requiring impedance control in the flex region

inputs.name: impedance-target
inputs.desc: Target impedance for flex-routed signals

outputs.name: flex-impedance-geometry
outputs.desc: Trace width and spacing for target impedance in the flex stackup, accounting for polyimide Dk and adhesive Dk

outputs.name: impedance-tolerance-in-flex
outputs.desc: Achievable impedance tolerance in flex (wider than rigid due to material variation and thinner dielectric)

outputs.name: flex-routing-rules
outputs.desc: Routing rules specific to flex: no trace on the outer bend surface, curved traces (no right angles), hatched ground planes

process: Calculate impedance using flex dielectric properties: polyimide has Dk around 3.2 to 3.5 (lower than FR-4's 4.2). Adhesive layers have Dk around 3.5 to 4.0. The effective Dk depends on the layer structure. For a microstrip on polyimide, Z0 will be higher than on FR-4 for the same geometry because the lower Dk reduces capacitance per unit length.

Expect wider impedance tolerance in flex: +/- 15% is typical for flex (vs +/- 10% for rigid). The thinner dielectric makes impedance more sensitive to thickness variation, and polyimide film has wider thickness tolerance than rigid laminate. If the protocol requires +/- 10%, the flex geometry must be designed with extra margin.

Route traces on the compression side (inner bend surface) when possible. Traces on the tension side (outer surface) experience direct tensile stress during bending and are more likely to crack. For single-sided flex, place copper on the inside of the bend.

Use hatched (crosshatched) ground planes instead of solid ground planes in flex regions. A solid copper plane makes the flex rigid and resistant to bending. A hatched ground plane (typically 50 to 70% copper coverage) maintains some reference plane integrity for impedance control while allowing the flex to bend. The impedance changes with hatch pattern: use the field solver to model the specific hatch geometry.

steps.description: Define and execute reliability testing for the flex design: bend testing, thermal cycling, and qualification criteria.

inputs.name: flex-classification
inputs.desc: Static, flex-to-install, or dynamic classification

inputs.name: minimum-bend-radius
inputs.desc: Design bend radius

inputs.name: transition-zone-design
inputs.desc: Transition zone geometry

inputs.name: bend-cycles
inputs.desc: Required cycle life

outputs.name: bend-test-specification
outputs.desc: Test method: mandrel radius, bend rate, number of cycles, pass/fail criteria (resistance change, visual inspection)

outputs.name: thermal-cycle-test
outputs.desc: Thermal cycling parameters: temperature range, dwell time, number of cycles, monitoring method

outputs.name: qualification-report
outputs.desc: Test results with pass/fail for each criterion, any failures with root cause analysis

process: Define the bend test per IPC-TM-650 2.4.3: mount the flex section on a mandrel at the minimum bend radius. Bend to the maximum angle at a controlled rate (1 cycle per second for dynamic flex). Monitor electrical continuity of all conductors during bending. Pass criteria: no resistance increase greater than 10% over the initial value for the required number of cycles.

Define thermal cycling per IPC-TM-650 2.6.7.2: cycle from -40C to +85C (or the product's operating range) with 10-minute dwells at each extreme. Minimum 500 cycles for consumer products, 1000 for industrial, 2000 for automotive. Monitor continuity after every 100 cycles. The rigid-to-flex transition zone is the most likely failure point.

For qualification, also test: peel strength of coverlay adhesion (IPC-TM-650 2.4.9), chemical resistance of coverlay (exposure to flux, cleaning solvents), and dimensional stability after reflow (flex material can shrink or bow during reflow soldering in the rigid sections).

If a bend test failure occurs: cross-section the failure point microscopically. Typical failure modes are copper cracking at the outer bend surface (bend radius too tight or wrong copper type), delamination at the adhesive interface (adhesion process issue), or cracking at the rigid-to-flex transition (stress concentration). Each failure mode has a different corrective action.

description: Set up and execute design rule verification: DRC, DFM, and signal integrity rule hierarchy, constraint-driven design, voltage clearance rules from IPC-2221, and a design review checklist.

steps.description: Establish the DRC, DFM, and signal integrity rule hierarchy and set up the EDA tool's constraint manager with net classes derived from signal requirements.

inputs.name: signal-classes
inputs.desc: All signal types with their impedance, speed, and spacing requirements

inputs.name: power-rails
inputs.desc: All power nets with voltage levels and current requirements

inputs.name: component-library
inputs.desc: Component footprints with pad sizes and spacing

outputs.name: net-class-definitions
outputs.desc: Net classes with assigned trace widths, spacing, via sizes, and impedance targets

outputs.name: rule-hierarchy
outputs.desc: Priority order: safety clearance > signal integrity > DFM > default routing rules

outputs.name: constraint-manager-setup
outputs.desc: EDA tool constraint configuration file or setup instructions for the defined rules

process: Define net classes by signal type: high-speed differential (USB, PCIe, Ethernet), high-speed single-ended (clock, JTAG TCK), general digital, analog, power, and high-voltage. Each class gets a set of rules: trace width (from impedance calculation), clearance to other classes (from crosstalk budget), via size (from current or impedance requirement), and length constraints.

Set the rule hierarchy: safety clearance rules (from voltage ratings) override all other rules. If two signals require 4 mil spacing for impedance but the voltage difference between them requires 8 mil per IPC-2221, the 8 mil rule wins. Signal integrity rules (impedance, length matching) override DFM rules. DFM rules (minimum annular ring, acid trap prevention) override default routing rules.

Configure the EDA tool's constraint manager: enter each net class with its rules. Assign every net to a class (no net should use default rules for a production design). Set differential pair constraints (impedance, spacing, length matching tolerance) and matched-length group constraints (DDR byte lanes, parallel buses).

Set up rule-checking automation: configure the EDA tool to run DRC continuously during routing (real-time DRC) for spacing, width, and connectivity rules. Signal integrity rules (impedance, length matching) can be checked interactively or in batch after routing. DFM rules should be checked before Gerber generation.

steps.description: Calculate electrical clearance and creepage distances from operating voltages using IPC-2221 and safety standards, and apply them as design rules.

inputs.name: operating-voltages
inputs.desc: All voltage levels present on the board, including transient voltages

inputs.name: pollution-degree
inputs.desc: Environmental contamination level (1 = sealed, 2 = normal indoor, 3 = conductive pollution possible)

inputs.name: safety-standard
inputs.desc: Applicable safety standard (IEC 62368-1, IEC 60950-1, UL 60950, etc.)

outputs.name: clearance-table
outputs.desc: Minimum clearance (through air) between each voltage pair, from IPC-2221 Table 6-1 and the applicable safety standard

outputs.name: creepage-table
outputs.desc: Minimum creepage (across surface) for safety-critical insulation barriers, from the safety standard

outputs.name: design-rules-for-clearance
outputs.desc: EDA constraint entries for voltage-based clearance rules between specific nets or net classes

process: Identify all voltage pairs that require clearance rules. This includes: power to ground, power to power (different rails), signal to signal (different voltage domains), and most critically, primary (mains-connected) to secondary (SELV) circuits. The primary-to-secondary barrier is a safety insulation barrier with specific clearance AND creepage requirements.

Calculate clearance from IPC-2221B Table 6-1: for internal conductors (conformal-coated or between layers), clearance is 0.1 mm + 0.1 mm per volt above 50V. For external conductors at sea level, bare board (no conformal coat), the requirements are more stringent. For example, 100V between bare external conductors at Pollution Degree 2 requires 0.4 mm clearance.

Calculate creepage from the safety standard: creepage depends on the voltage, pollution degree, material group (CTI of the PCB material), and the type of insulation (functional, basic, reinforced). Reinforced insulation (primary to secondary in a mains-powered device) typically requires 2x the basic insulation creepage. For FR-4 (Material Group IIIb), 240V reinforced insulation at Pollution Degree 2 requires approximately 5 mm creepage.

Implement as design rules: create net classes for primary-side and secondary-side nets. Set the clearance rule between these classes to the calculated value. For creepage, add a slot or cutout in the PCB between primary and secondary to increase the surface path length. A 1 mm wide slot adds the depth of the slot to the creepage path. Creepage is measured along the surface, including through slots.

steps.description: Run DFM checks specific to PCB fabrication: acid traps, copper balance, annular ring, and minimum feature sizes, fixing issues before Gerber release.

inputs.name: design-rules-for-clearance
inputs.desc: Clearance rules already applied

inputs.name: fabricator-capabilities
inputs.desc: Minimum feature sizes the chosen fabricator can produce

inputs.name: ipc-class-selection
inputs.desc: Selected IPC class for acceptance criteria

outputs.name: dfm-violation-list
outputs.desc: All DFM violations found, categorized by severity (fatal, major, minor)

outputs.name: acid-trap-locations
outputs.desc: Acute-angle intersections where etchant can pool, with fix instructions

outputs.name: copper-balance-analysis
outputs.desc: Copper coverage percentage on each layer, identifying layers with significant imbalance that could cause warping or uneven etching

process: Check minimum annular ring: the annular ring is the copper remaining around a drilled hole after drilling tolerance is applied. IPC-6012 Class 2 requires minimum 50 um (2 mil); Class 3 requires 50 um external and 25 um internal. The EDA tool calculates annular ring from pad size, drill size, and drill registration tolerance. If any via or through-hole pad has insufficient annular ring, increase the pad size or decrease the drill size.

Find acid traps: acute-angle intersections (< 90 degrees) between traces, or between traces and pads, trap etchant during the etching process. The trapped etchant continues etching after the rest of the board is clean, potentially opening the conductor. Check all trace intersections and pad connections. Fix by adding teardrops to pad connections (most EDA tools automate this) and rounding acute trace junctions.

Check copper balance: calculate the copper coverage percentage on each layer. If one side of the board has 80% copper and the other has 20%, the board will bow toward the low-copper side during lamination and reflow. Target copper coverage within 20% between the top and bottom halves of the stackup. Add copper thieving (non-functional copper fill) to sparse layers to improve balance.

Verify all feature sizes against the fabricator's capability: minimum trace width and space, minimum drill diameter, minimum pad size, maximum aspect ratio. Features below the fabricator's standard capability incur premium pricing or may be refused. Get the fabricator's capability document before starting the design, not after.

steps.description: Verify signal integrity rules: impedance, length matching, crosstalk, and stub lengths across all controlled nets.

inputs.name: net-class-definitions
inputs.desc: Constraint definitions with SI rules

inputs.name: rule-hierarchy
inputs.desc: Priority order for conflicting rules

inputs.name: constraint-manager-setup
inputs.desc: EDA tool configuration

outputs.name: impedance-verification-report
outputs.desc: Every controlled-impedance net: target, achieved (from field solver), and pass/fail

outputs.name: length-matching-report
outputs.desc: Every matched-length group: target tolerance, achieved mismatch, and pass/fail

outputs.name: crosstalk-report
outputs.desc: Near-end and far-end crosstalk between adjacent controlled nets, compared to budget

outputs.name: stub-length-report
outputs.desc: Via stub lengths for all high-speed nets, compared to the lambda/10 limit at the signal's bandwidth

process: Run impedance extraction on all controlled-impedance nets using the routed geometry and the fabricator-confirmed stackup. Compare extracted impedance to target. Flag any net where the impedance is outside the tolerance. Common causes: trace necked down near BGA pads (need to maintain width through the escape), reference plane void under the trace (need to check plane continuity).

Run length matching report for all matched groups: DDR byte lanes (each lane's data bits matched to its strobe, then all strobes matched to the clock), differential pairs (intra-pair matching), and bus groups (all bits of a parallel bus). Flag any group outside tolerance. Fix with serpentine length tuning.

Run crosstalk analysis on adjacent high-speed traces: extract near-end and far-end crosstalk from the 2D field solver at the actual routed spacing. Compare to the noise budget allocation for crosstalk. If crosstalk exceeds the budget, increase spacing between the victim and aggressor, or add a ground trace between them (a ground trace at the same layer, connected to the reference plane with vias, provides about 20 dB of additional isolation).

Calculate via stub lengths: for through-hole vias used by signals on inner layers, the unused portion of the via barrel is a stub that creates a resonance at f_res = c / (4 * L_stub * sqrt(Dk)). If this resonance frequency falls within the signal bandwidth, it causes insertion loss. The stub must be shorter than lambda/10 at the signal's bandwidth. If too long, use back-drilling to remove the stub (fabricator process) or use blind vias to avoid the stub entirely.

steps.description: Execute a structured design review using a checklist tied to the specific design's requirements and the fabricator's capabilities.

inputs.name: dfm-violation-list
inputs.desc: DFM violations to clear

inputs.name: impedance-verification-report
inputs.desc: SI verification results

inputs.name: length-matching-report
inputs.desc: Length matching results

inputs.name: clearance-table
inputs.desc: Voltage clearance verification

outputs.name: review-checklist-completed
outputs.desc: Every checklist item marked pass, fail, or waived with justification

outputs.name: open-issues-list
outputs.desc: Any items that could not be resolved with owner and target date

outputs.name: release-authorization
outputs.desc: Sign-off that the design is ready for Gerber generation and fabricator release

process: Walk through the checklist in order: schematic review items first (net connectivity, component values, power rail voltage/current), then layout review items (placement, routing, clearance, impedance, DFM), then output file review items (Gerber layers correct, drill file correct, pick-and-place file correct).

For each failed item: determine if it is a blocker (must fix before release) or a known-acceptable deviation (document the engineering justification). A DFM warning about minimum spacing on one trace may be acceptable if it is a non-critical signal and the fabricator has confirmed they can produce it. A safety clearance violation is always a blocker.

Verify the output files independently: generate Gerbers and view them in a Gerber viewer (not the EDA tool, which may show what is intended rather than what is generated). Check that every layer aligns, drill holes land on pads, solder mask openings expose the correct pads, and silkscreen text is readable and does not overlap pads.

Issue the release authorization with the signatures of the reviewer and the designer. Include the version, date, and a list of all waived items with justifications. This document becomes part of the design history file and is required for safety certification audits.
